Before the race, the driver will "reccy" the course - reconnoiter the course. They'll usually try to drive it twice.

During this, he tells the co-driver what the comments to tell him. The co-driver dutifully writes these down - but will have input at this stage. These are known as "pace notes." The most common is the Jemba system. 6 is barely a corner and 1 is a tight corner. So, you'll hear 4 left, over crest, 25, don't brake, 5 right, watch knoll.

You damned well better listen - as a general rule. The course may change. The co-driver may notice something. You may notice something. It may be unknown.

Not all drivers use a co-driver in all series. However, as a general rule, it's an agreed upon language and strategy to use during the stage. The driver will adhere to it as much as realistically possible.

In modernity, your helmets are connected with a wire so that audio is carried through to the driver's helmet. And, there's lots of little course corrections going on all the time. Also, you can't read pace notes. You could, but you'd have to learn. They're written in code for speed and simplicity. All those things mean something important. A driver may also have customized the language used.

I prefer a plainer language. 4 left, rise to knoll, 300, cut right, watch the bump, follow left hard, down for corner, brake at stump. Something like that.
